suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which increments match_count and saves, but UsersController#create runs validations twice (user.valid? at line 168, then user.save at line 172). WHY: every blocked signup attempt is counted twice, so the match_count stats this PR adds are wrong. HOW: don't write to the database from inside validation. Have the validator call a side-effect-free check and record the match once, e.g. after save fails or only on the save path.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: should_block? matches the email with an exact, case-sensitive where(email: email), and User does not normalize the email's case before validating. WHY: a blocked address can still sign up by changing its case (e.g. 'Bad@Spammers.org' when 'bad@spammers.org' is blocked). HOW: downcase emails when storing BlockedEmail records and when looking them up, e.g. where('lower(email) = ?', email.to_s.downcase).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: match_count is incremented as read, +1 in Ruby, then save, which is not atomic. WHY: when signup attempts for the same email run at the same time, both read the same value and one increment is lost. HOW: do an atomic SQL update, e.g. BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now]).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: should_block? reads match_count, increments it in Ruby, and saves the absolute value. Concurrent signup validations for the same blocked email can both read N and both write N+1, so matches are undercounted. Use an atomic SQL increment, for example update_all with `match_count = match_count + 1`.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: should_block? compares the submitted email against stored blocked emails with an exact, case-sensitive match, and User does not normalize email case before validation. As a result, a blocked address can still sign up by changing letter case (e.g. 'BAD@spammers.org' vs 'bad@spammers.org'). Lowercase the email on both sides, both when saving a BlockedEmail and when looking one up.

With the whitelist set to `gmail.com`, `user@gmail.com.evil.org` matches and gets past the whitelist. Anchoring the pattern at the end of the string makes the whole domain match exactly.

suggestions.label: security

WHY: Any external page or email can embed `` and silently lower or mute notifications on any topic for a logged-in victim. suggestions.label: bug

suggestions.suggestionContent: The English `unsubscribe_link` string now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`, but `@template_args` only gets that key when a caller passes it explicitly. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `TopicsController#unsubscribe` lowers a watching or tracking user only to `regular`, which still sends notifications for replies and mentions; it mutes the topic only if the user was already at regular or below. The page still tells every user they 'will stop receiving notifications', which is false for watching or tracking users. Change the wording to match what the code does, or show a different message for each resulting level.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `TopicUser.find_by` returns nil when the user has no row for this topic, and the code then calls `tu.notification_level`, which raises NoMethodError. suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `website_name` is added as a plain attribute but not to `untrusted_attributes`, so the `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` check that hides `website` for TL0 users seen by anonymous visitors never runs for it. WHY: anonymous visitors get the TL0 user's website host and path through `website_name`, and user.hbs renders it, which defeats the anti-spam hiding of new users' websites. HOW: add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (and delete the custom include method) so it is gated exactly like `website`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `include_website_name` has no trailing `?`, so ActiveModel::Serializers, which looks for `include_<attr>?`, never calls it. WHY: the intended condition is dead code and `website_name` is always serialized, as nil when the user has no website. HOW: rename it to `include_website_name?`.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: The parent and sibling checks compare raw dot-separated labels, so a top-level domain or other public suffix counts as the forum's own domain. For example, a website host of `com` matches `forum.example.com` because `'forum.example.com'.ends_with?('.com')`. Likewise, `evil.co.uk` counts as a sibling of `forum.co.uk`. In both cases a user-controlled path from a site the forum doesn't own is shown as if it were on the forum's domain. Require the website host to have at least two labels, or compare registrable domains using a public-suffix list.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: ActiveModel::Serializer only looks for `include_website_name?` (with a question mark) when deciding whether to include an attribute. As written, this method is never called, the `website.present?` gate never takes effect, and `website_name` is always serialized (as nil when there is no website). Rename it to `include_website_name?`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: ActiveModel::Serializers looks for include_website_name? (with a '?') to decide whether to include the attribute. Because this method is named without the '?', it is never called, and website_name is always serialized, so the method does not do what its name says. Rename it to include_website_name? so it actually controls inclusion.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The `include_website_name` method is missing its trailing `?`. The serializer only recognizes `include_website_name?`, so it ignores this method and always includes the `website_name` attribute. This is not a data exposure, because the value is a subset of the already-public `website` field.

suggestions.label: maintainability
suggestions.suggestionContent: `include_website_name` has no trailing `?`, so the serializer never uses it to decide whether to include the field. It is a dead predicate, and `website_name` runs for every user. The reviewer notes this causes no crash or corrupt data: with no website set, `URI("").host` is nil and the method returns nil.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Targets are now run through applyTemplateVariables (with request.filters) before splitting, and they go through it again later. Each split sub-request (`{ ...request, targets }`) is sent through datasource.runQuery -> DataSourceWithBackend.query, which calls applyTemplateVariables again with the same scopedVars and filters (DataSourceWithBackend.ts:185). WHY: addFilterAsLabelFilter (modifyQuery.ts:511) does not check for duplicates, so ad hoc filters on parsed or structured-metadata labels are added twice (e.g. `{app="x"} | json | level=`info` | level=`info``), and variable values containing `$` are expanded a second time. The non-split path interpolates only once, so the two paths now send different queries. HOW: Clear the ad hoc filters on the sub-requests (e.g. build them with `filters: undefined`) or skip the second interpolation, so each query is interpolated exactly once.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: runShardSplitQuery now applies applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters) up front, but the sharded sub-requests keep request.filters/scopedVars. datasource.runQuery -> DataSourceWithBackend.query then calls applyTemplateVariables on them again. WHY: Ad hoc filters on non-indexed labels are appended twice by addFilterAsLabelFilter, which does not check for duplicates, and `$` sequences inside already-interpolated values are re-expanded, so sharded queries differ from what the user built. HOW: Remove `filters` from the sub-requests passed to runQuery, or make sure the backend-layer interpolation is not applied a second time.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The `.filter((query) => query.expr)` check now runs on the raw expr before `applyTemplateVariables`, whereas before this PR it ran after interpolation. A query like '$SELECTOR' whose variable resolves to an empty string now passes the filter and reaches shard splitting and runQuery with an empty expr. Move the expr filter after the map so the check applies to the interpolated value.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: enableSqlExpressions assigns `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)` and returns false on both branches, so the flag lookup is dead code and the variable name means the opposite of its value. WHY: the code looks like a flag gate but ignores the flag; if someone changes the final `return false` to restore flag behavior, the inverted `enabled` makes the flag work backwards. HOW: make the kill switch explicit with a single `return false` and a comment, and drop the misleading flag lookup.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `enabled` is assigned `!h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, so it is true exactly when SQL expressions are disabled. The name therefore states the opposite of its value, and `if enabled { return false }` reads as disabling the feature when it is enabled. Rename it to `disabled`, or drop the negation, so the identifier matches what it holds.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions returns false on both branches, so ReadQuery rejects every SQL expression query as "not implemented" even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled globally. The feature flag can no longer turn the feature on. Return the flag's value instead.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Both branches of enableSqlExpressions return false, so ReadQuery rejects every SQL expression even when the sqlExpressions flag is on. Callers that enabled the flag used to get SQL queries parsed. Now they always get 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'. Return the flag value directly.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions computes the negated value of FlagSqlExpressions, but both branches return false, so the flag check is dead code. As a result, ReadQuery rejects SQL expressions even when the flag is enabled. The function should return the flag's value directly.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: TablesList now calls a stub that always returns an error, so existing parser tests (pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go) would break.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, which disables SQL expressions and would break existing tests.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The denial cache is checked before any permission source and is never invalidated when permissions change or a resource is created. WHY: If a Check on a UID runs before the dashboard/folder is created or before access is granted, the user keeps getting `Allowed:false` for the whole shortCacheTTL, even though the new permCache-miss database fallback would now allow it. That is the stale-deny behaviour this PR is meant to fix. HOW: Don't short-circuit on the denial entry when the database has never confirmed the resource exists. Or, simpler, drop the denial-cache short-circuit and rely on the refetch path, possibly with a much shorter TTL for denials.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: When the cached permission map exists but does not allow the resource, Check now ignores it and calls getIdentityPermissions, which always runs permissionStore.GetUserPermissions against the database. WHY: Each distinct denied resource (per user and action, per TTL window) now costs a full permission query, where before it cost none. Per-item checks over search/list results the user cannot access therefore cause O(N) database queries, and singleflight only merges concurrent calls with the same key. HOW: Refetch at most once per user+action within a short window, for example with a 'recently refreshed' marker on userPermCacheKey, instead of once per denied resource.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_', and resource UIDs can contain '_', so different (name, parent) pairs produce the same key (e.g. name='a_b',parent='' and name='a',parent='b_'). WHY: A cached denial for one resource is returned for a different resource, wrongly denying access for the TTL. HOW: Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or length-prefix or encode each component.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: newRemoteRBACClient still wraps the remote authz client in a 30s authzlib LocalCache, while only the in-proc client was switched to NoopCache. WHY: In standalone/remote deployments, Check and List results are still served from the client cache. Newly created dashboards and folders and fresh grants stay invisible for up to 30s, so the server-side refetch logic never runs. HOW: Use NoopCache for the remote client too, or a cache that does not store denied results.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment says the permCache entry allows access to the dashboard to show that it is never checked, but the entry is set to `false`, which does not grant access. Because the comment disagrees with the code, the test does not show that the denial cache wins over a cached allow: it would pass even if the denial-cache lookup were removed. Set the value to `true` so the code does what the comment says.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The test is meant to show that the denial cache wins over a cached allow, but it seeds permCache with `"dashboards:uid:dash1": false`, which denies access. With the permDenialCache lookup removed, Check would still return Allowed=false from the cached map or the store, so this test cannot catch a broken denial-cache path. Seed a real allow (`true`) so only the denial cache can make the result false.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_' and doesn't escape them, so (name="a_b", parent="") and (name="a", parent="b") produce the same key. A deny cached for one resource is then returned for a different resource the user may actually be allowed to access, until the TTL expires. Fix this by using a separator that can't appear in UIDs, or by escaping or length-prefixing each part.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The denial key joins name and parent with "_", but resource and folder UIDs can themselves contain "_", so different pairs map to the same key. For example, (name="a", parent="b_c") and (name="a_b", parent="c") both produce `..._a_b_c`, so a cached denial for one resource wrongly denies the other until the TTL expires. Use a separator that can't appear in UIDs, or a length-prefixed or escaped encoding of each field.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with "_", which UIDs may contain. For example, name="a_b"/parent="" and name="a"/parent="b" produce the same key, so a cached denial for one resource makes Check return Allowed:false for a different resource the user can access. Use a delimiter that UIDs can't contain, or a distinct, unambiguous prefix like ".perm_denial_", so the key identifies exactly one (name, parent) pair.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `userPermDenialCacheKey` joins name and parent with "_", and Grafana UIDs may contain "_". Different resources can therefore share one key: (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") both become "..._a_b_c". A denial cached for one resource is then returned in Check for the other, so a user who has permission is denied until the TTL expires; the fix is to use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or to encode the fields.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Debug log calls fire at Error level on every cleanup batch, including successful ones, and print the full list of IDs (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries). WHY: Normal cleanup runs flood the logs with fake errors and huge payloads, which can set off error-based alerts and hide real failures. HOW: Remove these calls, or switch them to r.log.Debug and log only the counts.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The cleanup ticker interval went from 10 minutes to 1 minute, but clean() still uses a 9-minute timeout sized for the 10-minute interval. WHY: Every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations) now runs 10x more often against the DB, and runs back-to-back whenever a pass takes more than a minute. This looks like a debugging change left in. HOW: Restore the 10-minute interval.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: On every database except SQLite, deleteByIDs binds one placeholder per ID, so the parameter count equals AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize. WHY: MySQL and Postgres cap a statement at 65535 placeholders, so a batch size above that now fails every cleanup run; the old subquery version had no bind parameters and worked. HOW: Split ids into chunks under the driver limit before building placeholders, or inline the int64 values for every dialect.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The SQLite inline IN list is built by calling fmt.Sprintf on the growing string once per ID. That is O(n²) copying and allocation in the batch size. WHY: At batch sizes like the 32767 used in the new test, each batch copies gigabytes of string data, which slows cleanup and puts heavy pressure on the GC. HOW: Build the list with strings.Builder and strconv.AppendInt.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: On every normal cleanup batch, this leftover debug statement writes the full list of annotation IDs (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32767) and the raw SQL condition to the error log. That leaks internal row identifiers and query text into production logs. Log only the count, at Debug level.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: In the MaxCount path, every batch writes the full slice of annotation IDs and the SQL condition (including the LIMIT/OFFSET) to the error log, even when nothing went wrong. This exposes internal identifiers and query structure in production logs. Log only the count, at Debug level.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags writes every annotation_tag ID in each batch, plus the raw subquery condition, to the error log on every cleanup cycle. This puts internal DB data into production logs where it doesn't belong. Log only the count, at Debug level.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Each subtest now seeds fresh annotations (line 116) and wipes the tables in t.Cleanup, so this case never runs the max-count cleanup a second time. It only checks that 3 annotations per type with MaxCount=3 deletes nothing. If a second run over-deleted, the case would still pass. suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The fail-fast exception for multiple crypto providers was replaced by sorting on order(), but DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200. A tie between them is now settled by ServiceLoader discovery order, and the loser is only logged at debug level. WHY: A FIPS deployment that accidentally also has the default (non-FIPS BouncyCastle) provider on the classpath used to fail at startup; now it can silently run with the non-FIPS provider. HOW: Keep throwing IllegalStateException when the two highest-ordered providers have the same order() value.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The test creates one EC key pair with the default KeyPairGenerator settings (a 256-bit curve) and uses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. WHY: The ES384 and ES512 cases never produce 48- or 66-byte r/s values or a DER sequence longer than 127 bytes, so the long-form length branches in ASN1Encoder.writeLength and ASN1Decoder.readLength are never tested and a bug there would go unnoticed. HOW: Generate a key pair on the matching curve (secp256r1, secp384r1, secp521r1) for each algorithm.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `int order()` is added to the public CryptoProvider SPI as an abstract method with no default. WHY: Any CryptoProvider implementation outside this repository stops compiling, and an already compiled one fails with AbstractMethodError when detectProvider calls CryptoProvider::order. HOW: Declare it as a default method that returns a base value, for example `default int order() { return 0; }`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The test only checks that R||S matches after a DER→RS→DER→RS round trip, so the two conversions are only compared with each other. If asn1derToConcatenatedRS swapped r and s or used the wrong offsets, the round trip would reproduce the same wrong bytes and the test would still pass. Verify the re-encoded DER with Signature.verify against the public key, and check rsConcat against the r/s values decoded independently from the JDK signature.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The single key pair comes from KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") with no curve set, which defaults to P-256, and is reused for ES384 and ES512. Those tests therefore never handle 48-byte or 66-byte (P-521) r/s values and only test zero-padding of 32-byte integers. A size-specific bug in integerToBytes or the length handling would not be caught. Generate a key pair on secp256r1, secp384r1 or secp521r1 to match each algorithm.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Default, FIPS and Elytron providers all return order() 200, so after the stable sort, foundProviders.get(0) is whichever one ServiceLoader finds first, i.e. it depends on classpath order. Before this change, having several providers threw an error. Now, if both FIPS and default BouncyCastle providers are on the classpath, one is picked silently and the debug log is the only sign of it. A FIPS deployment could end up running the non-FIPS provider. Keep the error for providers tied at the top order value.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: These two statements DER-encode r and s and then discard the encoders. The returned value is built from new encoders on lines 117-121, so this is dead computation, likely left over from copy-paste. Remove both lines.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: detectProvider() used to throw when more than one CryptoProvider was found, and callers relied on that to catch misconfiguration. Now Default, Elytron and FIPS all return order 200, so if two of them are present the winner depends on classpath order and the others are only mentioned in a debug log, which could mean a non-FIPS provider runs in a FIPS deployment. Keep the fail-fast error when the top providers have the same order, and only resolve by order when the orders differ.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: The check that threw on multiple providers was removed, and DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order 200. If the top-ranked providers have the same order, keep throwing the IllegalStateException.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The old code refused to start when several crypto providers were on the classpath. The new code sorts by order() and keeps the first, but DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200, so a tie is settled by ServiceLoader/classpath order and only a debug log mentions the ignored providers. suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: canManage() returns true when the caller has only the VIEW scope on all groups, because it passes AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW to hasPermission. WHY: GroupsResource (line 181) uses auth.groups().requireManage() to guard top-level group creation, so an admin granted only all-groups VIEW can create groups (privilege escalation). suggestions.label: bug

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new Javadoc for requireManageMembers was copied from requireManageMembership and still points to canManageMembership(GroupModel). suggestions.label: bug

suggestions.suggestionContent: Group resources are named after the group id (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup), but this loop returns groupResource.getId(), the resource's own UUID. suggestions.suggestionContent: Per-group resources are named by group ID, but this code passes `groupResource.getId()` (the resource UUID) to `hasPermission`, so `findByName` misses and the check falls back to the all-groups resource. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `MgmtPermissionsV2.groups()` now returns `GroupPermissionsV2`, but `GroupResource` still calls `isPermissionsEnabled`, `resource`, `getPermissions` and `setPermissionsEnabled` (lines 326–359) from its management-permissions endpoints. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The PR renumbers the exit codes (RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE 4→3, and 4 is reused for FEATURE_DISABLED), but testFeatureNotEnabled and testWrongVersions only check messages, not exit codes. WHY: The exit code is the documented contract for automation scripts, so a wrong or swapped value (for example, feature-disabled reported as recreate) would pass the suite. HOW: Assert `assertEquals(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED, cliResult.exitCode())` in testFeatureNotEnabled and `assertEquals(CompatibilityResult.RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE, result.exitCode())` after each incompatible check in testWrongVersions.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The PR makes exit code 4 (CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED) a documented contract for the feature-disabled case, but this test only checks the error text. It would still pass if the gate exited with 0 or with 3 (RECREATE), which would make automation such as the operator read the result wrongly. Assert `cliResult.exitCode()` equals `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: This test only asserts that a message is absent, so it would still pass if `--features=rolling-updates` were not honoured and the command stopped with the feature-disabled error. Add a positive assertion that the metadata command actually ran, such as `assertMessage("Metadata:")` or an exit-code check of 0.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: getCredential always calls getFederatedCredentialsStream first. For LDAP-federated users this runs LDAPStorageProvider.getCredentials, which queries LDAP and throws IllegalStateException when the LDAP object is not found. WHY: recovery-code login and the RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean page now fail with a 500 (and pay an LDAP round-trip on every call) for federated users whose recovery codes are stored locally, where before only local storage was read. HOW: check local stored credentials first and only fall back to the federated stream, or only consult the federated provider when it supports the recovery-codes type.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: when user storage accepts the new recovery codes, the local `createCredential` is skipped, and that call is the only place an existing local recovery-codes credential gets deleted. WHY: UserCredentialManager.isValid still runs the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider, so codes the user meant to replace by regenerating still authenticate. HOW: when userStorageCreated is true, remove any existing local recovery-codes credential.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: the user-storage path serializes the raw plaintext recovery codes (`generatedCodes`) into the UserCredentialModel, while the local path stores only the hashed codes from credentialModel. WHY: any user storage provider receives and may persist plaintext recovery codes, so a leak of the external store exposes working second-factor codes. HOW: pass the hashed credential data (credentialModel.getCredentialData()) to the user storage instead of the raw codes.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: the credential can now come from user storage, but when all codes are used it is still deleted with `removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`, which only acts on the local store. WHY: a federated credential (whose id may be null when built via createFromValues) is never removed from the user storage, so the exhausted credential stays configured. HOW: when the credential has a federation link or came from the federated stream, remove it through the storage provider (e.g. disableCredentialType) instead of removeStoredCredentialById.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The error log hard-codes the credential type as "recovery-codes", but RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE is "recovery-authn-codes". Anyone reading the log or searching for the type will be pointed at a type that does not exist. Use the constant so the message stays correct.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` can now return a credential from user storage (federated), but once all codes are used the authenticator still deletes it with `removeStoredCredentialById`. That call only removes credentials from the local Keycloak DB, so the federated credential stays in user storage and the user is still treated as configured for recovery codes. Remove it through a path that handles federated credentials too, e.g. `credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById` only when the credential is local, and `updateCredential`/`disableCredentialType` against user storage when it is federated.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: isValid returns true if the input matches any generated code (anyMatch), but the login page asks for one specific code number (getNextRecoveryAuthnCode). A user can enter any of their codes instead of the requested one and still pass, so this does not behave like the local provider. The check should compare the input only against the code at the expected (next unused) index.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: getCredentials builds a new model with createFromValues instead of returning the stored CredentialModel, so the id generated in updateCredential is not passed through. Anything downstream that relies on the credential id gets a different or null id, for example removeStoredCredentialById in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator or account credential listing. Set the id on the rebuilt model from myUser.recoveryCodes.getId().

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` now read the federated credential through `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`. They assume a successful `isValid` uses up the accepted code, so the next requested code number moves forward and `allCodesUsed()` can eventually be true. This `isValid` accepts any stored code and never removes it, so every login asks for code #0, codes can be replayed, and regeneration is never triggered. After a successful match, check the input against the requested next code and remove it from the stored JSON list.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on getattr(item, self.key), but the audit log endpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime', so the value is a datetime. WHY: build_cursor calls this key on the result rows and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError, so every non-empty optimized_pagination request returns a 500. HOW: Convert datetimes to epoch milliseconds, as DateTimePaginator.get_item_key does, or subclass DateTimePaginator.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value, and build_queryset puts it directly into a `datetime <= %s` filter for the '-datetime' key. WHY: Comparing an integer millisecond timestamp to a datetime column either fails in the database or filters the wrong rows, so following any next/prev cursor is broken. HOW: Convert the cursor value back to a UTC datetime, as DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: When enable_advanced_features is set, a client-supplied negative cursor offset is passed straight to queryset[start_offset:stop]. WHY: Django QuerySets reject negative indexing with ValueError/AssertionError, and paginate() only catches BadPaginationError, so a cursor like `0:-5:0` gives an unhandled 500. HOW: Reject negative offsets by raising BadPaginationError, or clamp them to 0.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: enable_advanced dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access on every request, and member can be None for non-superuser principals that pass OrganizationAuditPermission without an org membership. WHY: Because the line runs before the use_optimized check, those requests now raise AttributeError and return a 500 even when the default paginator would have been used. HOW: Check use_optimized first and guard against a missing member.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment says the Django ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically", but `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The comment states the reverse of what this branch actually does, so it presents a crashing path as safe. Correct the comment, or clamp the offset so the code matches the documented behaviour.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new comment in BasePaginator.get_result says passing a negative offset through for prev cursors is safe "because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions". Django querysets reject negative slice indices with a ValueError instead of handling them. The comment documents a guarantee that does not exist.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The endpoint passes order_by="-datetime" to OptimizedCursorPaginator, but that paginator's get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on the key value, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value. Those are numeric-key semantics, not DateTimePaginator's datetime handling. With optimized_pagination=true, any non-empty result raises TypeError when the cursor is built from a datetime. The integer cursor value would also be compared against the datetime column without conversion. Either make OptimizedCursorPaginator handle datetime keys the way DateTimePaginator does, or use DateTimePaginator for this datetime-ordered queryset.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: When a client sends a negative cursor offset (for example `0:-5:0`), this code slices `queryset[-5:...]`, and Django QuerySets raise an error on negative indexing, so the request fails with a 500. The comment says the ORM handles this, but it does not, and the `is_prev` branch skips the clamp in the same way. Always clamp the start index with `max(0, offset)` before slicing.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new clamp applies only to forward cursors, so a prev cursor with a negative offset (for example `0:-1:1`, which Cursor.from_string accepts) still slices the QuerySet with a negative start. Django raises on that, and the request returns a 500. Clamp the offset regardless of `is_prev`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The audit log endpoint uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime", but get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on a datetime object, which raises TypeError whenever results are returned. value_from_cursor also passes the raw integer cursor value into the datetime filter instead of converting it back the way DateTimePaginator does. The key handling needs to match DateTimePaginator's datetime-to-epoch conversion in both directions.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The audit log endpoint uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by='-datetime', so `getattr(item, self.key)` returns a datetime and `math.floor`/`math.ceil` raise a TypeError when the cursor is built. Any non-empty request on the optimized path therefore fails. Convert the datetime to an epoch value the way DateTimePaginator.get_item_key does.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: value_from_cursor returns the integer cursor value unchanged, and build_queryset compares it against the `datetime` column. Following pages are then filtered on a wrong or invalid value instead of the timestamp the cursor encodes. Convert the cursor value back into a datetime the same way DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: When advanced features are on and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start, and Django QuerySets reject that with an AssertionError or ValueError. A client-supplied cursor like `0:-5:0` therefore causes an unhandled exception and a 500. Clamp the offset to 0, or reject negative offsets.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The audit log endpoint uses OptimizedCursorPaginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, self.key)` returns a datetime and `math.floor`/`math.ceil` raise TypeError when `build_cursor` computes keys. As a result, every request with optimized pagination crashes. Convert the datetime to epoch milliseconds the same way DateTimePaginator does, and convert it back in `value_from_cursor`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: For `is_prev` cursors the offset is left unclamped, so a negative offset from a client cursor goes into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` and Django raises on the negative index, returning a 500 from every BasePaginator endpoint. Clamp the offset in both directions.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: _is_error_focused_query uses a plain substring check, so a query like '!event.type:error' or 'event.type:error OR event.type:transaction' is treated as errors-only. WHY: for allowlisted projects on the discover dataset, count() is rewritten to upsampled_count() for queries that exclude errors or include transactions, and the returned counts are wrong. HOW: parse the query with the event search parser and only return True when there is one positive, non-negated event.type:error filter with no OR branches.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: count() is rewritten to 'upsampled_count() as count', which always produces a result column named 'count'. With transformAliasToInputFormat=1, the serializer instead looks for the column 'count()', because resolve_axis_column uses the original query_columns in organization_events.py. WHY: for allowlisted error queries that use transformAliasToInputFormat, the series lookup misses and the endpoint returns empty or zero-filled data instead of the upsampled counts. HOW: make the alias of the rewritten column match whatever resolve_axis_column will look up, for example alias it to the original column name when transform_alias_to_input_format is enabled.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The 'no project IDs provided' check runs while the mocked allowlist is still `[]`, so the function returns False through the empty-allowlist check and never reaches the `if not project_ids` guard. If that guard were removed, `all()` over an empty list would return True and every query with no projects would be upsampled, yet this test would still pass. Set a non-empty allowlist before this check.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `_is_error_focused_query` uses a plain substring check, so the negated query `!event.type:error` also matches. That query means "exclude errors", but upsampling still turns on. On the discover dataset, count() then becomes `upsampled_count()` for a query that selects only non-error events (for example, transactions), so the counts returned are wrong. Parse the query, or at least require that the match is not preceded by `!`, before reporting the query as error-focused.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `final_columns` replaces `count()` with `upsampled_count() as count`, so the query result series is now keyed `count` (or an `upsampled_count` alias) rather than `count()`. The response serialization (`get_event_stats_data`, which handles multi-yAxis and top-events grouping) still uses the original `query_columns` to look up each series. As a result, multi-axis or top-events responses can drop the upsampled series or put it under the wrong key. Make the transformed column keep the alias that consumers expect (for example the `count()` result key), or map the results back to the original column names before returning.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `_is_error_focused_query` uses a substring test, so `!event.type:error` (and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`) also count as error-only queries. On the discover dataset this applies the `upsampled_count()` / `sample_weight` transform to non-error events, which breaks the rule that the transform only applies to errors. Match the filter as a whole, non-negated token instead of a substring.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Every strategy built by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker reuses the single factory-level self.queue_pool, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join()/terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown() on that shared pool. WHY: After the first partition rebalance, the next strategy submits into shut-down queues. queue.put raises ShutDown, the except in submit() marks the offset complete, and messages are committed without ever being processed. HOW: Create a new FixedQueuePool per create_with_partitions call, or stop shutting down the shared pool in close() and only shut it down in factory.shutdown().

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: _commit_loop calls the arroyo Commit callback from a background daemon thread instead of from the strategy's submit/poll on the main thread. WHY: arroyo's commit changes StreamProcessor state and commits offsets on the KafkaConsumer, which is not thread-safe, while the main thread is polling the same consumer at the same time. This can cause races, lost commits, or commits landing during a rebalance. HOW: Have the background thread (or poll()) compute committable offsets, then call self.commit_function inside poll() on the main thread.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Work queues are created as unbounded queue.Queue(), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never raises MessageRejected, so arroyo gets no backpressure. WHY: When processing falls behind (the slow-item case this PR targets), the consumer keeps pulling messages and buffering full Message objects in memory without limit, which can exhaust memory and cause a huge redelivery after a crash. HOW: Give each queue a maxsize and, in submit, use put_nowait and raise MessageRejected on queue.Full so arroyo retries the message.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: get_committable_offsets stops advancing at the first offset in range(start, max+1) that was never added to all_offsets. WHY: Kafka offsets can be non-contiguous (transaction control markers, compacted topics), so a single offset that is never delivered stops commits for that partition forever while all_offsets keeps growing. HOW: Walk the sorted list of seen offsets above last_committed and stop only at the first one that is still outstanding, instead of requiring every integer to be present.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False), so each worker exits its while loop after its current item instead of draining the queue. WHY: Items still in the queues are dropped at shutdown, which defeats the graceful drain that immediate=False is meant to provide and forces reprocessing on restart. HOW: Do not set worker.shutdown; let workers drain until get() raises queue.ShutDown.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing, but `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `complete_offset` in a `finally` block (line 149). That marks the offset complete even when `result_processor` raised, so the commit loop commits it anyway. Callers who trust this guarantee will assume failed messages get redelivered, but they are dropped after being logged.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The docstring promises "natural backpressure when queues fill up", but every work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize (line 185). As a result, `put` never blocks and the queues can never fill. A reader would wrongly expect memory to stay bounded when workers fall behind.

suggestions.suggestionContent: ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and passes it to every strategy that create_with_partitions builds, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() shut that shared pool down whenever partitions are revoked. After a rebalance, the new strategy submits to queues that are already shut down and whose workers have exited. submit() catches the resulting queue.ShutDown and marks the offset complete, so the message is dropped but its offset is still committed. The pool's lifetime belongs to the factory (factory.shutdown() already shuts it down), so the strategy should only stop its own commit thread.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The docstring says processing errors must not block offset commits, but the test asserts that nothing was committed (`len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`). It only waits ~0.2s after processing, while _commit_loop runs about once a second, so it passes because the commit hasn't happened yet and would also pass if a failed item blocked commits forever. Wait for the commit loop and assert `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The queue_pool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every strategy that create_with_partitions builds. close() and terminate() still call queue_pool.shutdown(), so after a rebalance the new strategy submits into shut-down queues. queue.put raises ShutDown, the except block in submit() marks the offset complete, and the message is committed without being processed. Leave pool shutdown to the factory's shutdown(), and only stop the commit thread here.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The loop requires every integer offset between last_committed+1 and max to appear in all_offsets. Kafka partitions can legitimately skip offsets (transaction markers, compaction), so one missing offset stops commits for that partition forever. Messages arrive in order, so the committable offset should be the largest seen offset below min(outstanding), or max(all_offsets) when nothing is outstanding.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The FixedQueuePool is created once by ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every strategy that `create_with_partitions` returns, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()`/`join()` shut it down. After the first partition rebalance, the new strategy submits to dead queues: `put` raises `queue.ShutDown`, `submit()` swallows it and marks the offset complete, so offsets are committed for messages that were never processed. Leave pool shutdown to `factory.shutdown()`, which owns the pool, and only stop the commit thread in the strategy.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `_commit_loop` calls the arroyo `commit` callable from its own daemon thread, but that callable stages and commits offsets on the KafkaConsumer, which the StreamProcessor thread drives at the same time. This races with the consumer's own poll/commit/revocation, and the KafkaConsumer is not safe for concurrent use; it can also commit offsets for partitions that were just revoked. Compute the committable offsets in the commit thread if you like, but call `commit_function` from `poll()`/`submit()` on the processor thread.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The script now runs ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE on segment keys that consumers on the previous version created with SADD as plain sets, and those keys live for up to redis_ttl (3600s). WHY: During a rolling deploy, or for up to an hour after it, Redis returns WRONGTYPE for these keys, so the EVALSHA fails and p.execute() in process_spans raises, crashing the consumer batch. HOW: Use a new key prefix for the sorted-set buffers (e.g. `span-buf:z:`) so old and new data never collide, or check the key with TYPE and migrate or skip legacy sets.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: ZUNIONSTORE is called without AGGREGATE, so it defaults to SUM and adds the scores of a payload that appears in both sets. WHY: A duplicate span (e.g. a Kafka redelivery) ends up with a score of about twice its end timestamp, so ZPOPMIN never evicts it and the eviction no longer follows end time. HOW: Pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) so a duplicate member keeps its real timestamp.
